title: A-V-D
hookLine: avodah means both work and worship

cards: Moses stands in front of Pharaoh with a message he will carry again and again: "Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness." Serve.
A strange word to bring to a king who already has the Hebrews building his store cities. They're already serving every day: mud, straw, brick, field. Moses isn't asking for them to stop serving.
He's asking for them to serve someone else. In Hebrew, the brickwork and the worship use the same root.

teach.h: TO DRESS IT: WORKING THE SOIL.
teach.b: A-V-D. Ayin, vet, dalet. Avodah: work, labor, service, worship.
Turn it four ways. First, back to yesterday's garden: "to dress it and to keep it." Keep was shamar.
Dress is from this root: to work the soil, to till it. Before any altar or temple, avodah in the Eden story means digging. Second, Egypt.
Early in Exodus comes a hard line: "they made their lives bitter with hard bondage." Bondage there is avodah. The same root names the worst thing in the story.
Let my people go, that they may serve me: serve is this root again. The exodus doesn't move the people from work to nothing. It moves their avodah from Pharaoh to God.

And in Pirkei Avot, Shimon the Righteous teaches that the world stands on three things: Torah, avodah and acts of lovingkindness. Avodah there means the service in the Temple. Fourth, after the Temple.
The rabbis read Deuteronomy's call "to serve him with all your heart" and ask what kind of service happens in the heart.
Their answer, in tractate Taanit: prayer. Digging, slavery, offerings, prayer: one root runs through all of them. So its question isn't whether you work.
It's who and what the work is for.

how: Jews call prayer avodah she-ba-lev, the service of the heart, after the rabbis' reading of Deuteronomy 11:13; on Yom Kippur the synagogue recalls the Temple's service in a section of prayers called the Avodah.

o: a payment or wage earned for labor
work, service and worship, all in one root
rest from work, the opposite of labor

s: the Hebrew for slavery in Egypt and the word for worship share a root
avodah names both the hard bondage and the service of God.
Moses asks Pharaoh to let the people go so they can stop serving
"that they may serve me": the service moves from Pharaoh to God.
avodah in Pirkei Avot means a person's day job
there it means the service in the Temple.

games.q: you're Moses, in front of Pharaoh. what's the message you carry?
o: let my people go, that they may rest.
let my people go, that they may serve me.
let my people go back home.
games.why: "Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness." not an end to service: a change of master.

practice: Bring to mind the next ordinary task waiting for you: a spreadsheet, a load of laundry, a shift, a diaper.

Ask the root's question, who is this for, maybe a customer, a child, a tired coworker, a stranger you'll never meet, and let the task belong to them for a minute. If you pray, you can offer the work to God before you start.

wordCard.voice: A-V-D. Ayin, vet, dalet: avodah, the work of the soil, the bondage in Egypt, the Temple service, and prayer, the service of the heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: work, labor, service, and worship.

carryVoice: Your line: work is worship. The question is who the work is for. Back tomorrow, same hill.
